chunks: Muhammad ibn 'Isa narrated from 'Umar ibn Ibrahim al-Sabiri, from Hujr ibn Zaydah, from a man, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him, 'O son of the Messenger of Allah, I have a need.' He said, 'Meet me at Mecca.' I said again, 'O son of the Messenger of Allah, I have a need.' He said, 'Present your need.' I said, 'O son of the Messenger of Allah, I have committed a sin between myself and Allah which no one else knows of, so it weighs heavily on me, and I revere you too much to mention it to you.' He said, 'When the Day of Resurrection comes, and Allah takes account of His believing servant, He stops him for his sins, one by one, then He forgives him. He is not made known to it, neither a close angel nor a chosen Prophet.' 'Umar ibn Ibrahim said, 'I was informed by more than one person that he said: And He conceals from him some of his sins that he dislikes to be questioned about.' He said, 'And He says to his misdeeds,
They are the ones whose evil deeds Allah will change into good deeds, and Allah is Oft-forgiving, Merciful.
He said, 'And that is the saying of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted.'
ai.seo_question: How does Allah handle the sins of a believer on the Day of Judgment according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) elucidates the intimate nature of individual reckoning, emphasizing that Allah conceals the believer's sins from even the highest angels and prophets, thereby preserving their dignity. It underscores the transformative mercy where specific sins are converted into good deeds, a concept rooted in Surah Al-Furqan but also resonating with the broader theme of divine forgiveness in Surah Az-Zumar. This narrative serves as a source of hope for believers, illustrating that sincere repentance can lead to a complete elevation of status rather than mere pardon.
